source.title: Severe Necrotizing Fasciitis in a Human Immunodeficiency Virus-Positive Patient Caused by Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus
source.source_type: clinical case report with molecular isolate characterization and narrative literature review

extraction_metadata.scope_note: Index-case clinical course, microbiology, molecular characterization, Figure 1, Table 1, Table 2 summary, limitations, conclusions, and funding were atomized. Bibliographic entries were not atomized as primary evidence.

atoms.canonical_statement: The report describes an unusually severe MRSA necrotizing fasciitis case in a patient with previously undiagnosed HIV/AIDS and molecularly characterizes the infecting isolate.
The index patient was a 36-year-old Hispanic man with no previously recognized significant medical conditions.
Two weeks before admission, the patient had been treated with clindamycin for right axillary hidradenitis after a self-reported spider bite, but the skin infection did not resolve.

exposures.details: prior outpatient treatment for right axillary hidradenitis

atoms.canonical_statement: At emergency-department presentation, the patient had severe right-arm soft-tissue findings and was diagnosed with severe cellulitis, septic shock, and possible necrotizing fasciitis.
The initial white blood cell count was 1,600/µL.
The initial blood pressure was 58/32 mm Hg with pulse 130/min and temperature 99.4°F.
Empirical antimicrobial therapy was initiated with vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and clindamycin.
Emergency surgical exploration occurred within 24 hours of admission; extensive necrosis led to right-arm amputation and extensive chest-wall debridement.
Sputum and blood cultures collected before empirical therapy and intraoperative wound cultures grew MRSA.
After MRSA susceptibility results, therapy was changed to vancomycin, imipenem/cilastatin, rifampin, and voriconazole.
Despite initial improvement, septic shock persisted and necrotizing fasciitis spread to both chest walls, the right abdomen, and the right back.
After transfer to a tertiary-care hospital, the patient underwent nine additional debridement procedures; subsequent tissues grew rare MRSA with the same susceptibility pattern.
The patient gradually improved and was discharged to a rehabilitation center.
HIV infection was newly diagnosed during the hospitalization.
At discharge, the CD4+ cell count was reported as less than 20 cells/mm³.

population.label: Index patient with newly diagnosed HIV infection

atoms.canonical_statement: At discharge, the HIV viral load was 358,000 copies/mL.

population.label: Index patient with newly diagnosed HIV infection

atoms.canonical_statement: After the life-threatening MRSA infection resolved, the prescribed HIV-related regimen included tenofovir, lamivudine, atazanavir, ritonavir, dapsone, and azithromycin.
One month later, the CD4+ count was 192 cells/mm³.

population.label: Index patient with newly diagnosed HIV infection

quantitative_result.original_result_text: One month later, his CD4+ count was 192 cells/mm3

atoms.canonical_statement: Figure 1A shows nonviable myocytes and adipocytes in necrotic tissue with inflammatory cells infiltrating along major fascial planes and individual muscle fibers.
Figure 1B shows a thrombosed artery within necrotic soft tissue.
No organisms were seen on Gram staining of the necrotic tissue.
Molecular genotyping of the peripheral-blood isolate was consistent with USA300, and spa sequencing identified spa type 1 associated with multilocus sequence type 8.
Multiplex PCR detected SCCmec IVa, the arginine catabolic mobile element, and lukS-lukF genes encoding Panton-Valentine leukocidin.
Western immunoblotting confirmed expression of alpha-hemolysin and PVL toxin by the isolate.
The authors identified 19 other English-language reported cases of MRSA necrotizing fasciitis, of which only one patient was HIV positive.
USA300 was documented in the index case and five of the 19 previously reported MRSA necrotizing fasciitis cases summarized in Table 2.
Table 2 contains many prior cases with unknown HIV status, MRSA bacteremia status, and/or genotype, limiting comparison across published cases.
The authors conclude that USA300 MRSA should be considered among pathogens that can cause necrotizing fasciitis, including in patients with HIV/AIDS.
The report emphasizes that apparently benign MRSA skin and soft-tissue infections can progress rapidly to potentially fatal illness.
The authors state that epidemiologic data and experimental models had not unambiguously demonstrated a direct role for PVL or ACME in invasive disease.

The therapeutic significance of constitutive clindamycin resistance and increased vancomycin MICs was described as uncertain; the authors only speculated that this profile may have contributed to treatment failure and progression.
The article is a single case report with a narrative English-language literature review and therefore cannot establish treatment efficacy, causal virulence mechanisms, or population-level risk.
The work was supported in part by American Heart Association grant 0775045N.
